meta.blurb: A retired dietitian with a vegetable patch has one rule for his neighbour Lena. A link is not proof. Over one year she learns to cook more plants, one simple meal at a time, and to question the headlines.
meta.bible: Lena: a young woman who decides in January to cook and eat more plants; curious, practical and a little stubborn. Mr Bashir: her neighbour, a retired Dietitian with a vegetable patch; patient, funny, careful with evidence, and always says that a link is not proof. Jonas: Lena's brother, who has a birthday barbecue in summer. Maya: Jonas's young daughter, who refuses Broccoli. The story runs from January to December in Lena's kitchen, her small garden, the market and the shops. Plants: vegetables, fruit, beans, Lentils, Lentil, Porridge, Chickpeas, Pulses, Legumes, whole grains, nuts and seeds. Fibre: the indigestible part of plants; many national guides advise about thirty grams a day for adults, and most adults eat less. World Health Organization: advises at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, free sugars under ten percent of energy, and under five grams of salt a day; its cancer agency in 2015 classed processed meat as a cause of bowel cancer and red meat as a probable one. Microbes, Microbiome, Bacteria: the tiny living things in the large intestine. Tofu, Tempeh, Soya, Soy: foods from soya beans. Warfarin: a blood-thinning medicine; Vitamin K, Folate, Lycopene, Beta-carotene, Vitamin B12, Vitamin C, Vitamin D, Iron, Calcium, Iodine, Omega-3. United Kingdom, Mediterranean, Asian, Sauerkraut, Kimchi, Yoghurt, Detox. Observational studies show links, not proof. Safety facts: dried red kidney beans must be soaked and boiled hard for at least ten minutes; nut allergies can be serious; fully plant-based eaters need vitamin B12 from fortified food or a supplement; anyone with a health condition, a pregnancy, a child to feed or on medicine should ask a doctor or registered dietitian. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, practical and gently funny; science is hedged where it is uncertain; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice. New people: Dara is Lena's friend, fully plant-based for years, who teaches her to cook dal and takes a vitamin B12 supplement. Tom is Lena's colleague, who sends her food headlines. Mrs Costa runs the market stall where Lena buys vegetables. Dr Patel is Lena's doctor. Mr Bashir is past seventy, takes vitamin D and B12 on professional advice, and still has the old pressure cooker he lends Lena. Foods and food words used in the book: Spinach, Kale, Chard, Cabbage, Carrots, Parsnips, Leeks, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Cumin, Turmeric, Paprika, Coriander, Ginger, Garlic, Chilli, Barley, Quinoa, Buckwheat, Bulgur, Oats, Hummus, Tahini, Edamame, Miso, Kefir, Rhubarb, Courgettes, Radishes, Beetroot, Gluten, Coeliac, Cholesterol, Potassium, Sodium, Oxalate, Protein, Probiotics, Prebiotics, Flax, Chia, Walnuts, Almonds, Olive, Rapeseed, Margarine, Cereals, Sugars, Sweeteners, Supplements, Multivitamin, Zinc, Selenium, Anaemia, Isoflavones, Pressure, Superfoods, Dietitian, Nutritionist, Registered, Folic, Acid, Eggs, Dairy, Fish, Pasta, Tomatoes, Peppers, Mushrooms, Onions, Beans, Peas, Apples, Oranges, Berries, Bananas, Pesto, Dal, Tarka, Aquafaba. Evidence words: Randomised, Trial, Trials, Confounders, Headline, Headlines, Absolute, Relative, Peer, Review, Adjust, Pigments, Carotenoids, Anthocyanins, Chlorophyll. Chapter facts: PREDIMED was a large trial in Spain; its paper was corrected and published again in 2018 with similar findings. In 2015 the cancer agency also said that its classes describe how strong the evidence is, not how big the risk is.
chapters: A Fridge Full of Ready Meals
The Rainbow on the Market Stall
Fats, Oils and the Meat Question

beats.scene: Lena stands before an open fridge holding a ready meal on a grey evening
beats.summary: On a grey January evening Lena finds only ready meals in her fridge and decides to change.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir leans on his spade beside a winter vegetable patch
beats.summary: Over the garden fence Lena asks her neighbour Mr Bashir, a retired dietitian, for help.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir pours tea at a kitchen table beside a bowl of beans
beats.summary: Mr Bashir's first lesson is that the goal is more plants, not only plants.

beats.scene: Vegetables, fruit, beans, grains, nuts and seeds spread across a wooden table
beats.summary: Plants means vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils, whole grains, nuts and seeds, a family much wider than salad.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir sketches a plate divided into three parts on a paper napkin
beats.summary: A simple plate has about half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains and a quarter protein.

beats.scene: Five words are written in capital letters on the back of a napkin
beats.summary: Mr Bashir gives Lena his one rule: a link is not proof.

beats.scene: Lena writes in a new notebook beside a plate of toast
beats.summary: Lena keeps a food diary for a week, writing down everything she eats.

beats.scene: Lena frowns at a notebook page full of bread, pasta and cheese
beats.summary: The diary shows meals built on bread, pasta and cheese, with vegetables almost missing.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir taps a notebook page and smiles at Lena
beats.summary: Mr Bashir says a diary is a map, not a judge, and suggests one small change.

beats.scene: Lena unpacks bags of carrots, cabbage, peas and rice onto her counter
beats.summary: Lena shops for vegetables and cooks a first stir-fry that evening.

beats.scene: A chalkboard shows the number 400 beside a ring of fruit and vegetables
beats.summary: The World Health Organization advises at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, about five portions.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir lines up an apple, two plums and a bowl of salad
beats.summary: A portion is about a medium apple, two plums, a dessert bowl of salad or three spoonfuls of cooked vegetables.

beats.scene: A baked potato sits apart from a plate of colourful vegetables
beats.summary: Potatoes do not count towards the daily total in most guides, though they are a good food.

beats.scene: A long supermarket queue with mostly empty fruit and vegetable baskets
beats.summary: Surveys show that most adults eat less fruit and vegetables than experts advise.

beats.scene: Lena stirs frozen peas into a pan of pasta
beats.summary: Lena adds one vegetable to every meal rather than taking things away.

beats.scene: A bowl of apples and oranges sits on a kitchen table
beats.summary: Fruit in sight and biscuits out of sight changes what Lena reaches for.

beats.scene: Mrs Costa weighs leeks and carrots at a winter market stall
beats.summary: At the market Lena learns that seasonal vegetables are fresher and usually cheaper.

beats.scene: Lena fans away steam from an overcooked pot of cabbage
beats.summary: Overcooked cabbage smells strong because long cooking releases sulphur compounds.

beats.scene: Lena rinses apples and carrots under a running tap
beats.summary: Lena washes her produce, and learns that the benefits of eating it outweigh worries about pesticide traces.

beats.scene: Lena writes a number four in her notebook while Mr Bashir lifts his mug
beats.summary: Lena reaches four portions on a Friday, which Mr Bashir calls progress, not a medal.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir writes the word fibre on a chalkboard and underlines it twice
beats.summary: Fibre is the indigestible part of plant foods, and it is found only in plants.

beats.scene: Lena reads the label on a loaf of bread with a pencil in hand
beats.summary: Adults are often advised to eat about thirty grams of fibre a day, and most eat less.

beats.scene: Oats, beans, apples and a seeded loaf are sorted into two groups
beats.summary: Soluble fibre forms a gel in water, while insoluble fibre adds bulk.

beats.scene: Lena drinks a glass of water beside a bowl of beans and oats
beats.summary: Fibre keeps the bowels moving and helps people feel full, and extra water helps it work.

beats.scene: A bowl of oats, lentils and apples stands on a sunny windowsill
beats.summary: Soluble fibre can help to lower cholesterol in the blood.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir taps a page of studies while Lena reads over his shoulder
beats.summary: Fibre-rich diets are linked with lower risks of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and bowel cancer, but a link is not proof.

beats.scene: A chalk drawing of the gut filled with tiny dots
beats.summary: The large intestine holds trillions of microbes, together called the gut microbiome.

beats.scene: A chalk diagram shows microbes turning fibre into small molecules
beats.summary: Microbes ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids that seem to nourish the cells of the gut.

beats.scene: Lena reads an advertisement for a home gut test with a doubtful frown
beats.summary: Gut tests are sold with big promises, but the science is young and cannot yet give reliable personal advice.

beats.scene: A sheet of paper with a tally of plants is stuck to a fridge
beats.summary: A survey linked eating many kinds of plants with more varied gut microbes, so Lena starts a tally.

beats.scene: Glass jars of dried beans, lentils and chickpeas line a kitchen shelf
beats.summary: Beans, lentils and chickpeas, called pulses or legumes, are cheap and rich in fibre and protein.

beats.scene: Peas, peanuts and many kinds of beans fill small bowls on a table
beats.summary: Peas, peanuts and soya beans are all legumes, and cooks around the world use many kinds.

beats.scene: A tin of chickpeas stands beside a jar of dried ones
beats.summary: Tinned beans are ready to eat after a rinse, while dried beans cost less but need soaking and cooking.

beats.scene: Lena stirs red lentils, onion and garlic in a pot on the stove
beats.summary: Lena cooks red lentil soup with onion, garlic, cumin and lemon, with no soaking needed.

beats.scene: Lena eats a bowl of golden soup while steam rises
beats.summary: The soup smells wonderful and Mr Bashir approves it over the fence.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir holds up a finger beside a pot of boiling kidney beans
beats.summary: Dried red kidney beans contain a natural toxin and must be soaked and boiled hard for ten minutes.

beats.scene: Lena laughs and holds her stomach beside a pot of beans
beats.summary: Beans can cause wind at first because gut bacteria ferment the fibre, so Lena goes slowly.

beats.scene: Lena mashes chickpeas in a bowl beside a lemon and a jar of tahini
beats.summary: Lena makes hummus from tinned chickpeas, lemon, garlic and tahini.

beats.scene: A saucepan of chilli with black beans sits beside a slice of toast
beats.summary: Lena slips pulses into pasta sauces, soups, chilli and even breakfast beans on toast.

beats.scene: Lena holds her phone over a bowl of golden soup
beats.summary: Lena sends Jonas a photo of her soup and her tally shows sixteen plants in a week.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir cuts open a loaf beside a drawing of a grain
beats.summary: A whole grain has all its parts: the outer bran, the germ and the starchy middle.

beats.scene: White flour and brown wholemeal flour sit in two bowls side by side
beats.summary: Refined grains such as white flour and white rice have lost the bran and germ in milling.

beats.scene: A loaf of wholemeal bread beside a bag of brown rice on a counter
beats.summary: Lena swaps refined grains for whole ones one meal at a time.

beats.scene: Small bowls of oats, barley, rye, bulgur and quinoa on a shelf
beats.summary: Many grains and grain-like seeds count as whole grains when they are eaten intact.

beats.scene: A bowl of porridge topped with berries and nuts on a sunny table
beats.summary: Lena starts her mornings with porridge, fruit, nuts and seeds.

beats.scene: A box of oats with a small heart drawn on the label
beats.summary: Oats contain beta-glucan, a soluble fibre that can help to lower cholesterol.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir points to a page of results beside a bowl of oats
beats.summary: Large studies link whole grains with lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, but cannot prove grains alone are the cause.

beats.scene: Lena turns over a loaf of bread to read its ingredients
beats.summary: A brown colour does not prove a loaf is whole grain, so Lena reads the ingredient list.

beats.scene: A baker's loaf and a bag of rye flour beside a gluten-free sign
beats.summary: People with coeliac disease must avoid gluten, but others gain nothing proven from avoiding it.

beats.scene: A big pot of barley cooks on the stove beside a pile of herbs
beats.summary: Cooking a pot of barley for the week leaves Lena feeling full for much longer.

beats.scene: Tom shows Lena a phone with a bold headline about a miracle seed
beats.summary: Lena's colleague Tom shows her a headline claiming that a miracle seed halves the risk of heart attack.

beats.scene: Two chalk circles joined by an arrow on Mr Bashir's board
beats.summary: A link between a food and an illness can mean the food causes it, the illness changes the diet, or something else causes both.

beats.scene: A long line of people of all ages fills in food questionnaires
beats.summary: Observational studies follow large groups for years, which gives size but cannot remove every difference between people.

beats.scene: A chart on a board compares two groups with different habits
beats.summary: People who eat well often smoke less and exercise more, and researchers can only adjust for what they measured.

beats.scene: Two groups of volunteers receive different meals in a research kitchen
beats.summary: A randomised trial lets chance decide who gets which treatment, which removes many hidden differences.

beats.scene: A calendar with many years crossed off beside a single plate
beats.summary: Diet trials are hard because people cannot hide what they eat and diseases take years to appear.

beats.scene: Four puzzle pieces labelled lab, trial, survey and biology fit together
beats.summary: When lab work, trials, surveys and biology agree, confidence grows.

beats.scene: A chalk drawing shows one in a thousand doubling to two in a thousand
beats.summary: A doubled risk can still be small, and headlines rarely say how large the risk was before.

beats.scene: Lena pins a handwritten list of questions to her fridge
beats.summary: Lena pins questions to her fridge: people or mice, how many, who paid and has anyone repeated it.

beats.scene: Lena reads a small study report while Tom looks sheepish
beats.summary: The study behind the headline was small and measured only one blood test, so the headline was far bigger than the facts.

beats.scene: A market stall piled with red, orange, green and purple vegetables
beats.summary: Colourful vegetables owe their colours to natural pigments, and a plate of many colours holds many different substances.

beats.scene: A tub of bright green powder sits beside a plain cabbage
beats.summary: Variety matters more than any single superfood, a word that is mostly used to sell things.

beats.scene: Frozen blueberries and blackberries pour into a bowl of porridge
beats.summary: Berries and purple vegetables contain anthocyanins, and cheap frozen berries keep most of their goodness.

beats.scene: Lena washes bunches of spinach, kale and chard in a sink
beats.summary: Leafy greens are rich in fibre, folate and vitamin K, and are cheap in season.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir holds up one finger beside a pile of dark leaves
beats.summary: People who take the blood-thinning medicine warfarin should ask their doctor before changing how much leafy green they eat.

beats.scene: A tray of cauliflower florets roasts golden with paprika
beats.summary: Broccoli, cabbage and their relatives are linked in some studies with lower cancer risk, but a link is not proof.

beats.scene: Lena pours green water from steamed peas into a jug
beats.summary: Long boiling can leave water-soluble vitamins in the pan, while steaming and roasting keep more.

beats.scene: A salad glistens beside a bottle of olive oil and ripe tomatoes
beats.summary: Cooking can help the body absorb lycopene and beta-carotene, and a little oil helps further.

beats.scene: Sliced onions turn golden in a wide pan
beats.summary: Slowly cooked onions and garlic make the tasty base of countless plant-based dishes.

beats.scene: Mrs Costa hands Lena a big bunch of chard, laughing
beats.summary: Lena's tally reaches twenty different plants in a week, and she celebrates at the market.

beats.scene: A freezer drawer packed with bags of peas, spinach and sweetcorn
beats.summary: Frozen vegetables are picked, prepared and frozen within hours, so they keep most of their nutrients.

beats.scene: A lorry unloads crates of vegetables beside a shop display
beats.summary: Fresh vegetables that spend days in transport and storage can lose some vitamin C.

beats.scene: Lena rinses tinned beans in a sieve under the tap
beats.summary: Tinned tomatoes, beans and sweetcorn are useful, especially with no added salt or sugar.

beats.scene: A small jar of raisins and dried apricots stands on a counter
beats.summary: Dried fruit counts as a portion at about 30 grams, but its sugar is concentrated.

beats.scene: A whole orange stands beside a glass of orange juice
beats.summary: Pressing an orange removes most of its fibre and frees its sugar.

beats.scene: A can of fizzy drink beside twelve spoonfuls of sugar
beats.summary: Free sugars should stay under ten percent of energy, about 50 grams for a typical adult.

beats.scene: A blender full of fruit beside a bowl of whole fruit
beats.summary: Blending fruit breaks open its cells, so some guides count part of the sugar as free sugar.

beats.scene: A hand holds a small handful of walnuts and almonds
beats.summary: A small daily handful of nuts is linked with a lower risk of heart disease.

beats.scene: A bowl of plain nuts beside a note warning about allergies
beats.summary: Nuts are rich in energy, allergies can be serious and whole nuts are a choking risk for young children.

beats.scene: Jars of seeds and peanut butter line a kitchen shelf
beats.summary: Seeds and plain nut butters add fibre, minerals and healthy fats to Lena's meals.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir labels three chalk boxes unsaturated, saturated and trans
beats.summary: Fat is not the enemy: the body needs some, and the kind of fat matters most.

beats.scene: A bottle of olive oil beside a block of butter on a counter
beats.summary: Olive oil, nuts and seeds are rich in unsaturated fat, while butter, cheese and fatty meat have more saturated fat.

beats.scene: A jar of coconut oil and a bottle of palm oil on a shelf
beats.summary: Coconut and palm oils come from plants but are high in saturated fat.

beats.scene: A heart drawn in chalk beside a bottle of olive oil
beats.summary: Swapping saturated fat for unsaturated fat lowers harmful cholesterol, but swapping it for refined carbohydrates does not help.

beats.scene: Lena reads a label that lists partially hydrogenated oil
beats.summary: Industrial trans fats are the worst kind for the heart, and Lena checks her labels.

beats.scene: Lena measures a spoonful of oil into a frying pan
beats.summary: Oil is very rich in energy, so Lena measures it with a spoon.

beats.scene: A newspaper headline about bacon and sausages lies on a table
beats.summary: In 2015 the World Health Organization's cancer agency classed processed meat as a cause of bowel cancer and red meat as a probable cause.

beats.scene: A chalk chart shows two dots of very different sizes in one circle
beats.summary: The classification shows how strong the evidence is, not how large the risk is.

beats.scene: A small sausage on a plate beside a big pile of vegetables
beats.summary: Health advice is to eat less red and processed meat, and Lena lets beans and vegetables do more of the work.

beats.scene: A tin of sardines beside a boiled egg on wholemeal toast
beats.summary: Fish and eggs can fit in a plant-rich diet because the aim is plants first, not plants only.

beats.scene: Beans, lentils, tofu, nuts and grains arranged in rows on a board
beats.summary: Plants contain plenty of protein, and it does not need to be combined at every meal.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir points at a simple chart of protein foods on his board
beats.summary: Most adults need a little under one gram of protein per kilogram of body weight and many already eat more.

beats.scene: Lena presses a block of tofu between two plates
beats.summary: Lena learns to press and marinate tofu until it turns golden and savoury.

beats.scene: Cakes of tempeh, a tub of miso and a bowl of edamame in pods
beats.summary: Tempeh, miso and edamame are traditional soya foods.

beats.scene: Lena frowns at a phone screen while Mr Bashir shakes his head kindly
beats.summary: Moderate amounts of soya foods appear safe for most people, though some people should ask their doctor.

beats.scene: Two packets of vegetable burgers sit side by side with their labels showing
beats.summary: Meat substitutes vary widely, from simple and nutritious to salty and heavily processed.

beats.scene: Lena sorts snacks, fizzy drinks and ready meals on a counter
beats.summary: Ultra-processed foods are industrial products made with ingredients rarely found in a home kitchen.

beats.scene: Twenty people eat at long tables in a bright research kitchen
beats.summary: Studies link ultra-processed diets with poorer health, but the cause is still debated.

beats.scene: Lena studies a long ingredient list on a packet in a supermarket aisle
beats.summary: Ingredients are listed by weight, and short lists of familiar words are usually a good sign.

beats.scene: A handwritten card reading mostly plants, mostly whole, mostly happy on a fridge
beats.summary: Lena's rule is to cook mostly from whole foods without making it a test of purity.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir writes the number five on his chalkboard beside a teaspoon
beats.summary: Too much salt raises blood pressure, and the World Health Organization advises under 5 grams a day.

beats.scene: Lena reads salt figures on a loaf, a sauce jar and a soup can
beats.summary: Most salt is hidden in bread, sauces, soups, cheese, processed meat and takeaways.

beats.scene: Lena tastes a spoonful of soup with a thoughtful expression
beats.summary: The taste for salt adjusts within weeks if it is reduced slowly.

beats.scene: A salt shaker beside bowls of fresh herbs and sliced lemons
beats.summary: Lemon, vinegar, garlic, herbs, spices and umami foods add flavour without salt.

beats.scene: A bowl of beans, spinach and bananas on a table
beats.summary: Potassium in vegetables, fruit and beans helps balance salt, though people with kidney disease should ask their doctor.

beats.scene: A jar of tomato soup beside a pile of sugar cubes
beats.summary: Sugar hides in many savoury foods such as sauces, soups, cereals and yoghurts.

beats.scene: Lena copies the names of sugars from a label into her notebook
beats.summary: Sugar has many names on labels, such as glucose syrup, dextrose and maltose.

beats.scene: A slice of cake on a plate beside a bowl of fruit
beats.summary: Treats are part of life, so Lena keeps her Sunday cake.

beats.scene: A glass of sparkling water with lemon beside a can of diet drink
beats.summary: In 2023 the World Health Organization advised against sweeteners for weight control.

beats.scene: A pot of tomato sauce bubbles beside an empty jar and a basil plant
beats.summary: Lena makes tomato sauce from scratch and finds it cheaper, fresher and less sugary than the jar.

beats.scene: Lena digs a neglected corner of her garden while Mr Bashir watches
beats.summary: In June Lena turns a neglected corner of her garden into a vegetable bed, with a borrowed spade and compost.

beats.scene: Trays of young pea plants and packets of seeds on a garden table
beats.summary: Lena chooses easy plants, radishes, salad leaves, beans, courgettes and herbs, and Mr Bashir gives her young pea plants.

beats.scene: A chalk drawing of bean roots with little nodules in the soil
beats.summary: Bacteria on bean roots turn nitrogen from the air into plant food, so beans help to feed the soil.

beats.scene: A slug crawls across a half-eaten lettuce in the early morning
beats.summary: Slugs eat Lena's lettuces, and she learns that every gardener loses some.

beats.scene: Pots of mint, basil, parsley and chives beside a kitchen door
beats.summary: Herbs grow easily in pots, and mint needs a pot of its own because it spreads.

beats.scene: Lena carries a watering can through a golden evening garden
beats.summary: Gardening is gentle exercise and brings fresh air and daylight.

beats.scene: Mr Bashir cuts large green rhubarb leaves away from pink stalks
beats.summary: Rhubarb stalks are safe to cook but the leaves are poisonous.

beats.scene: Lena splits a pea pod open in the sunshine
beats.summary: Peas eaten fresh from the plant taste sweet, and most of the first harvest never reaches the kitchen.

beats.scene: A small bowl of radishes and salad leaves on a wooden table
beats.summary: After four weeks Lena makes a salad from her own radishes, leaves and herbs.

beats.scene: Lena and Mr Bashir eat at a small table among vegetable beds
beats.summary: On the longest evening of the year Lena and Mr Bashir eat dinner in the garden.

beats.scene: Lena adds up a pile of shopping receipts on her kitchen table
beats.summary: Lena finds that she spends less than before, though prices vary and substitutes can be costly.

beats.scene: Bags of dried beans, oats and rice beside a pile of cabbages
beats.summary: Dried beans, lentils, oats, rice, cabbage, carrots, onions and bananas are among the cheapest foods.

beats.scene: Two shopping baskets, one full of plain foods and one of packets
beats.summary: Meat, fish, branded convenience foods and snacks were where Lena's money used to go.

beats.scene: A handwritten shopping list on the fridge under a carrot-shaped magnet
beats.summary: Planning a week of meals and writing a list means fewer snacks and less waste.

beats.scene: A pot of soup made from broccoli stalks and soft carrots
beats.summary: Lena makes soup from stalks and soft vegetables instead of throwing them away.

beats.scene: Lena writes dates on freezer boxes with a marker pen
beats.summary: A use-by date is about safety and a best-before date is about quality, and the freezer saves bread and fruit.

beats.scene: Rows of labelled boxes of soup and stew stacked in a freezer
beats.summary: Batch cooking on Sundays fills the freezer with ready meals.

beats.scene: A card with food safety rules is stuck inside a cupboard door
beats.summary: Batch cooking needs quick cooling, short fridge times, thorough reheating and special care with rice.

beats.scene: Lena looks at Mr Bashir's old pressure cooker on her stove
beats.summary: A sharp knife, a big pot and a blender are enough, and a pressure cooker cooks dried beans quickly.

beats.scene: A steaming bowl of soup beside a loaf on a late evening
beats.summary: On a tired Wednesday a frozen soup becomes dinner in ten minutes.

beats.scene: A shelf of colourful spice jars beside a bunch of fresh herbs
beats.summary: Lena buys one new spice a week, and her cooking improves.

beats.scene: Whole cumin seeds sizzle in hot oil in a small pan
beats.summary: Warming whole spices in hot oil before adding onions makes the flavour deeper.

beats.scene: Bowls of dal, hummus, tofu soup and a bean stew on a table
beats.summary: Many great cuisines built delicious food on plants and flavour.

beats.scene: Dara arrives at Lena's door with a small jar of spices
beats.summary: Lena's friend Dara, who eats no animal foods, offers to teach her to make dal.

beats.scene: Dara and Lena stir a pot of golden lentil dal together
beats.summary: Dara and Lena cook a golden red lentil dal with cumin, ginger, garlic and tomatoes.

beats.scene: Dara and Lena talk at a candlelit table over empty bowls
beats.summary: Dara explains why she is fully plant-based, and they agree that a meal can be shared without agreeing about everything.

beats.scene: A small pile of yellow turmeric powder beside a wooden spoon
beats.summary: Turmeric is a lovely spice, but there is little good proof that a pinch is a cure.

beats.scene: Fresh ginger, garlic and red chillies on a chopping board
beats.summary: Ginger, garlic and chilli add flavour cheaply and may have interesting health effects still being studied.

beats.scene: A bean salad with tomatoes and herbs on an outdoor table
beats.summary: In July Lena makes cold dishes with beans, tomatoes, herbs and lemon.

beats.scene: Lena holds her phone, looking surprised, beside a bowl of bitter leaves
beats.summary: Lena learns to soften bitter leaves, and Jonas invites her to his birthday barbecue.

beats.scene: Lena arrives at a garden party carrying a bean salad and skewers
beats.summary: Lena brings a bean salad, vegetable skewers and corn to her brother Jonas's birthday barbecue.

beats.scene: A guest asks Lena a question while holding a paper plate
beats.summary: A guest asks whether she has become a vegan, and Lena says she is simply eating more plants.

beats.scene: A plate with vegetable skewers, bean salad, corn and one piece of chicken
beats.summary: Lena takes vegetables and a little chicken, because flexibility works better than strict rules.

beats.scene: Jonas turns chicken on a grill beside separate plates for raw meat
beats.summary: Safe barbecuing means cooking meat through, separating raw and cooked, and not leaving food out for too long.

beats.scene: Vegetable skewers brown on a barbecue grill over low flames
beats.summary: Heavily charred meat produces chemicals of concern, so gentle cooking is wiser.

beats.scene: Lena holds a glass of sparkling water with lemon and ice
beats.summary: No amount of alcohol is completely safe, and the heart benefit of red wine is doubtful.

beats.scene: A small girl pushes a bowl of salad away and holds up bread
beats.summary: Five-year-old Maya refuses every green thing and asks for plain bread.

beats.scene: An empty tray of skewers beside a half-eaten bowl of watermelon
beats.summary: The vegetable skewers, corn and watermelon are the first food to disappear.

beats.scene: Jonas and Lena talk quietly in a kitchen doorway
beats.summary: Jonas says his cholesterol is high, and Lena sends him to a doctor or dietitian while offering her recipes.

beats.scene: A sleeping girl on a blanket under an apple tree at sunset
beats.summary: Lena ends the day with birthday cake, knowing the best diet is one you can enjoy and keep.

beats.scene: A bottle of fortified plant milk beside a small bottle of tablets
beats.summary: Vitamin B12 is made by bacteria and is not reliably found in plants, so fully plant-based eaters need fortified food or a supplement.

Over the garden fence, Lena finds Mr Bashir leaning on his spade, and she tells him her plan. He is a retired dietitian with a prize vegetable patch, and he says he has waited years for someone to ask him.
On Saturday, Lena sits at Mr Bashir's kitchen table with a mug of tea and a bowl of beans. His first lesson is short: the goal is to eat more plants, not to give up everything else.
Plants, Mr Bashir explains, are vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils, whole grains, nuts and seeds. It is a huge and colourful family of foods, and a salad is only a small corner of it.

Many national food guides suggest a plate that is about half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains and a quarter protein. Mr Bashir draws it on a paper napkin, and Lena sticks it to her fridge door.
Before she leaves, Mr Bashir writes five words on the back of the napkin: a link is not proof. He promises to repeat them often, because they are the most important rule in the study of food.
Mr Bashir suggests that Lena should look before she changes anything, so she buys a notebook. For one week she writes down every meal, snack and drink, even the biscuits.
On the eighth day, Lena sits down and reads her notebook carefully from the very beginning. Her meals are mostly bread, pasta and cheese, and vegetables are almost missing.
Lena feels a little embarrassed, but Mr Bashir only smiles and taps the page. A diary is not a judge, he says, but a map that shows exactly where to start.

For the first small change, they agree that Lena will add one extra vegetable to her dinner. That afternoon she comes home from the shop with heavy bags, and she cooks a big vegetable stir-fry with rice.
The World Health Organization advises eating at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables every day. Mr Bashir says that this works out at about five portions, each of about 80 grams.
Mr Bashir shows Lena what a portion looks like: one medium apple, two plums, or a dessert bowl of salad. Three heaped spoonfuls of cooked vegetables or peas also make one portion, he says.
In most national guides, potatoes do not count towards the five portions, because they act as a starchy food, like bread. They are still a good food, he says, and they are cheap and filling.
Surveys in many countries show that most adults eat less fruit and vegetables than the experts advise. Mr Bashir says that this worries him more than it surprises him, because it is so common.

Lena decides to add one extra vegetable to every meal, because Mr Bashir says that small changes are easier. She stirs peas into her pasta, spinach into her scrambled eggs and grated carrot into her tomato sauce.
Lena keeps a bowl of apples and oranges in the middle of the table, where she cannot miss it. Mr Bashir says that food we can see is the food we tend to eat, and the biscuit tin goes into a cupboard.

A whole grain still has all of its parts: the outer bran, the inner germ and the starchy middle. The bran and the germ hold much of the fibre, vitamins and minerals, so Mr Bashir calls them the best parts.

Lena folded the napkin into her pocket without understanding it, and the months ahead would slowly show her what it meant.

Before changing anything, Mr Bashir suggested, it is wise to look at what one actually eats, so Lena bought a cheap notebook that evening. For a whole week she wrote down every meal, snack and drink, including the biscuits that she ate standing up in the kitchen. It was harder than she had expected, because writing a thing down makes one far more honest about it.

On the eighth day Lena sat down with her notebook and read it from beginning to end, as one might read a stranger's diary. Almost every meal was built from bread, pasta and cheese, and the vegetables appeared only as a garnish, a few slices of tomato here and a leaf of lettuce there. It was an honest picture, and she found it more interesting than embarrassing, because it showed her exactly where to begin.

Mr Bashir read the notebook slowly, nodding now and then, and he did not say a single critical word. A food diary, he explained, is not a judge but a map, and a map is useful precisely because it shows where you are standing. His advice was modest: choose one small change, such as adding a vegetable to every evening meal, and let it settle before choosing another.

That afternoon Lena came home from the shop with heavy bags full of carrots, onions, cabbage, frozen peas and a sack of brown rice, and she moved the ready meals to the freezer for emergencies. The stir-fry that she cooked for supper was simple and slightly lopsided, but it was bright with colour and it was entirely hers. As she ate it, she realised that she had not looked at her phone once, which was an unplanned and pleasant benefit.

The World Health Organization advises eating at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, which works out at about five portions of 80 grams each. Mr Bashir wrote the number on his kitchen chalkboard in large figures, because he suspected that most people had heard it a hundred times without ever measuring it against their own plate. It is a modest target and a rule of thumb rather than a magic line, he said, but it makes a useful place to start.

Mr Bashir showed her what a single portion looks like by pointing around his kitchen: one medium apple, two plums, a dessert bowl of salad leaves or three heaped spoonfuls of cooked vegetables would each count as one. Lena was surprised by how small the portions were, and she began to see that five of them were not the impossible mountain she had imagined. The trick, he said, was to stop thinking about the number and to start thinking about the next meal.

In most national guides, potatoes do not count towards the daily total, because they behave in the body like a starchy food, rather like bread or rice. This does not make them bad, Mr Bashir hastened to add, and a baked potato with its skin on is a cheap, filling and nourishing food in its own right. Beans and fruit juice, by contrast, count in some countries, but only once a day, however much of them a person eats.

Surveys in many countries have found that most adults eat less than the recommended amount of fruit and vegetables, and Mr Bashir finds the fact more worrying than surprising. People who eat more of them tend to live longer in large studies, he said, although a tendency is not the same as proof. Even so, the habit of eating more vegetables does little harm and plenty of good, and it seemed to him one of the safest bets in the whole of nutrition.

Lena decided to start by adding rather than taking away, and so she stirred frozen peas into her pasta, folded spinach into her scrambled eggs and grated a carrot into her tomato sauce. None of these changes required a new recipe or any special skill, and none of them tasted of virtue. By the end of the week she was adding a vegetable to every meal without having to think about it.

She moved the biscuit tin to a high cupboard and placed a bowl of apples and oranges in the middle of the kitchen table, where it was impossible to ignore. Mr Bashir, who approved of the experiment, told her that people tend to eat what is easy to reach and easy to see, and that willpower is greatly overrated. Within a few days, the bowl was emptying faster than the biscuit tin ever had.

On Saturday morning, Lena walked to the market and met Mrs Costa, a cheerful woman who had sold vegetables from the same stall for thirty years. In winter, Mrs Costa told her, the best buys are the vegetables that are in season, such as cabbages, leeks, carrots, parsnips and oranges, because they are fresher and usually cheaper. Lena left with two heavy bags and a free bunch of parsley, and with a promise that she would come back the following week.

Lena's first attempt at cabbage was a disaster: she boiled it for half an hour, and the whole kitchen smelled like a school canteen. Mr Bashir, who had been called in to help, explained that long cooking releases smelly sulphur compounds, whereas a few minutes in a hot pan keeps the leaves sweet and bright. The second cabbage, shredded and fried quickly with garlic, disappeared in a single sitting.

Lena washed every piece of fruit and vegetable under running water before she ate it, a habit that Mr Bashir called sensible, if only for the dirt. Some people worry about pesticide traces, he admitted, but most experts agree that the benefits of eating fruit and vegetables far outweigh that worry, whether the food is organic or not. The point, he said, is to eat more of them, and an anxious shopper who ends up eating fewer of them has gained nothing.

By the end of the second week, Lena managed to eat four portions of fruit and vegetables on a single Friday, and she wrote the number in her notebook with a flourish. Mr Bashir lifted his mug of tea in a small celebration and said that this was progress, not a medal, and that tomorrow she would be allowed a biscuit like anybody else. She laughed, because she had begun to suspect that he enjoyed teaching quite as much as she enjoyed learning.

Fibre is the tough, indigestible part of plant foods, found in vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts and seeds, and it is not found in meat, fish, eggs or dairy products. Mr Bashir wrote the word on his chalkboard and underlined it twice, because he believed that it was the most neglected nutrient on the modern plate. Lena, who had never thought of fibre as an ingredient, felt a small flicker of curiosity.

Some national guidelines, including those of the United Kingdom, advise adults to eat about thirty grams of fibre a day, yet the average adult eats considerably less. Lena spent an evening with a pencil, adding up the numbers on the labels of her bread, her cereal and her tins, and discovered with a small groan that she was nowhere near the target. Mr Bashir only laughed and said that most people begin in exactly the same place.

There are two main kinds of fibre, Mr Bashir explained, and most plant foods contain a mixture of both. Soluble fibre, found in oats, beans, apples and citrus fruit, dissolves into a soft gel in water, whereas insoluble fibre, found in whole grains, nuts and the skins of vegetables, adds bulk and moves things along. The distinction matters less in the kitchen than in the textbook, he added, since a varied diet supplies both without any special effort.

Fibre does several useful things at once: it keeps the bowels moving regularly, and it helps people to feel full for longer after a meal. As the amount of fibre in a diet rises, he advised, so should the amount of water, and the change is best made gradually to give the gut time to adapt. A sudden jump from almost none to a great deal, he warned with a grimace, is something that the stomach will not forgive.

In its soluble form, found in oats, beans, lentils and fruit, fibre can also help to lower the level of cholesterol in the blood, which is good news for the heart and arteries. The effect is real but modest, Mr Bashir said, and it works best as part of a pattern of eating rather than as a single heroic spoonful of oat bran. Lena, who had always thought of cholesterol as a villain, learned that the body needs some of it, and that the trouble lies in having too much of one particular kind.

Many large studies have linked diets rich in fibre with a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and bowel cancer. Mr Bashir paused when he said it, because a link, as he had warned her, is not the same as proof. Even so, he added, the pattern has appeared in many countries and many kinds of research, and that consistency is hard for a sensible person to ignore.

Mr Bashir drew the large intestine on his kitchen chalkboard and filled it with tiny dots, each of which, he said, stood for millions of living things. The gut is home to trillions of microbes, mostly bacteria, and together they make up what scientists call the gut microbiome. Lena looked at the dots and felt, for the first time in her life, rather crowded.

When these microbes ferment fibre, they produce short-chain fatty acids, substances that seem to nourish the cells lining the gut and that may influence other parts of the body as well. Mr Bashir called the process a quiet partnership: the plant provides the food, the microbes do the work, and the person gets some of the benefit. Researchers are still mapping how much each species matters, he added, which is why the details change from year to year.

A company that sold home tests promised to read Lena's gut microbes and to tell her exactly what to eat, and she showed the advertisement to Mr Bashir with some excitement. He read it carefully, and he explained that the science of the microbiome is young and exciting, but that most researchers believe such tests cannot yet give reliable personal advice. Anyone who promises simple miracles from the field, he said, is running well ahead of the evidence.

In one large survey, people who ate more than thirty different plant foods a week had more varied gut microbes than people who ate ten or fewer. It was only a survey and so showed a link rather than proof, but Mr Bashir liked the idea, because it rewards variety instead of perfection, and every kitchen can offer variety. Lena stuck a sheet of paper to her fridge and began a tally of every different plant she ate, counting herbs, nuts and grains, and by Sunday evening it had reached eleven.

On a shelf above Mr Bashir's cooker stood a row of big glass jars, each filled with dried beans, lentils or chickpeas in a different shade of brown, red and gold. These foods, which together are called pulses or legumes, are among the cheapest and most useful in the world, because they supply fibre and protein for very little money. Lena, who had always thought of beans as something for camping trips, began to look at her own kitchen shelves differently.

The family is far larger than most people realise: peas, peanuts and soya beans all belong to it, and so do borlotti, black, butter and haricot beans, as well as the lentils of India and the chickpeas of the Mediterranean. Cooks in almost every country have built great dishes around them, from Mexican refried beans to Ethiopian lentil stews and the baked beans of a British breakfast. Lena decided on the spot to try a new kind every week, and Mr Bashir, delighted, lent her three of his jars.

Tinned beans, Mr Bashir explained, are already cooked and need nothing more than a rinse, which makes them ideal for a busy evening. Dried beans cost even less and keep for years in a cupboard, although they must be soaked and then simmered until they are tender, and the water they were soaked in should be thrown away. Lena bought both kinds, on the principle that a cook should never be without a quick option and a cheap one.

For her first recipe, Lena fried a chopped onion and two cloves of garlic in a little oil, stirred in a cupful of red lentils, a spoonful of cumin and some water, and left the pot to simmer. Twenty minutes later it had turned into a thick golden soup, and she had not needed to soak, drain or measure anything with any great care. A squeeze of lemon at the end brightened the flavour in a way that she could not quite explain.

The kitchen filled with a warm and comforting smell that she did not associate with health food at all, and she ate two bowls before she remembered to be proud of herself. Mr Bashir, tasting a spoonful over the garden fence, declared it the perfect first dish and pronounced the lemon a masterstroke. It cost, Lena calculated, about as much as one takeaway coffee, and it had fed her for three meals.

Mr Bashir then added a safety note that he considered non-negotiable: dried red kidney beans contain a natural toxin, so they must be soaked, drained and then boiled hard for at least ten minutes before they are eaten. Tinned kidney beans have already been cooked and are perfectly safe, but a slow cooker may not get hot enough to destroy the toxin in dried ones. Lentils, fortunately, are far more forgiving and need no soaking at all, which is one more reason to begin with them.

After a few days of bean-heavy meals, Lena discovered the best-known side effect of a plant-rich diet, which is a great deal of wind. Mr Bashir, quite unembarrassed, explained that gut bacteria simply ferment the extra fibre, and that most people's guts adapt within a few weeks if the change is made gradually. He advised small portions at first, plenty of water and patience, and he added that anyone with stomach trouble that does not settle should ask a doctor.

On Sunday, Lena drained a tin of chickpeas and mashed them with lemon juice, garlic, olive oil and a spoonful of tahini until the mixture was smooth and pale. She tasted it, added a little more lemon, and realised that she had just made something that she had been buying in small, expensive tubs for years. Spread on wholemeal bread with a handful of crisp carrot sticks, it made a lunch that was cheap, filling and wholly her own.

Within a fortnight, Lena was slipping pulses into almost everything: red lentils dissolved into her pasta sauce, white beans thickened her soups, and a tin of black beans turned a pot of chilli into a family-sized feast. Baked beans on toast, Mr Bashir assured her, were also perfectly respectable, provided that she chose a tin with less sugar and salt. He called the whole family of foods the quiet workhorses of a healthy kitchen.

Lena sent her brother Jonas a photograph of her lentil soup, and he replied within a minute with a joke about rabbits and a request for the recipe. Smiling at the telephone, she looked at the tally on her fridge, which now showed sixteen different plants in a single week. She could not have said exactly when the project had stopped feeling like a duty, but she was fairly sure that it had.

A whole grain, Mr Bashir explained, still has all of its parts: the tough outer bran, the small nutritious germ and the starchy endosperm that surrounds it. The bran and the germ hold much of the fibre, along with many vitamins and minerals, and they are precisely what a mill removes when it makes white flour. Lena pictured a seed with its coat on, and thought that it made good sense to eat the whole thing.

Refined grains, such as white flour and white rice, have lost most of their bran and germ in the process of milling, which makes them last longer on the shelf and gives them a softer taste. In some countries, certain vitamins and minerals are added back to white flour by law, but the fibre is mostly gone. The difference, he said, is rather like the one between a book and its summary: the main idea survives, but a great deal of the detail has been lost.

Lena did not change everything at once, because Mr Bashir had taught her that slow changes are the ones that stay. She swapped one meal at a time, putting wholemeal bread in her sandwiches, brown rice under her curry and wholewheat pasta on her Friday plate. The change in taste was smaller than she had feared, and the change in how long she felt full was larger than she had expected.

Many grains besides wheat count as whole grains when they are eaten intact, and Mr Bashir listed them with relish: oats, barley, rye, brown rice, bulgur, millet and even popcorn. Quinoa and buckwheat are botanically seeds rather than grains, but cooks treat them alike, and they are every bit as useful. Lena bought a small bag of each, and her cupboard began to look like a shop in a market town.

Her new breakfast was a bowl of porridge made with oats, milk and a pinch of cinnamon, topped with chopped fruit, a few nuts and a spoonful of seeds. It took five minutes to cook, it cost less than the cereal she used to buy, and it kept her satisfied until lunchtime. For the first time in years, Lena found that she was looking forward to the morning.

Oats contain a soluble fibre called beta-glucan, which can help to lower the level of cholesterol in the blood, and health authorities in several places allow this claim on packets of oats. The effect is modest, Mr Bashir cautioned, and it works best as part of a wider pattern of healthy eating rather than as a single miracle ingredient. Lena, who liked the idea of a miracle ingredient that cost so little, took the point with good grace.

Many large studies in different countries have linked eating whole grains with a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes. They are mostly observational, however, and they cannot show that the grains alone are the cause, because people who choose whole grains often live healthier lives in other ways. Mr Bashir smiled when he said this, because it was exactly the point that he had been waiting to make.

In the bread aisle, Lena learned that a brown colour proves nothing, because some brown loaves are mostly white flour with a little colouring added, and that words such as multigrain and wheat are no guarantee either. The safest method, Mr Bashir had told her, is to turn the loaf over and check that the word whole or wholemeal appears first on the list of ingredients. She read a dozen labels that morning, feeling slightly ridiculous, and went home with a loaf that passed the test.

Some people cannot eat gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley and rye, because they have a condition called coeliac disease, in which gluten damages the lining of the gut. Mr Bashir was firm that anyone who suspects the condition should ask a doctor for a test before cutting gluten out, since the test only works while gluten is still in the diet. For everyone else, he added, there is no proven benefit in a gluten-free diet, and whole grains are better left on the plate.

On Sunday, Lena cooked a large pot of barley, and through the following days she stirred it into soups, mixed it with roasted vegetables and served it cold in salads with lemon and herbs. By Thursday she had noticed something odd: she felt comfortably full for much longer after lunch than she used to, and the three o'clock craving for biscuits had quietly disappeared. Mr Bashir, when she told him, only nodded and said that fibre does that, and that he had been trying to tell her so for weeks.

At work, Tom held out his phone to Lena and read a headline aloud in the voice of a television announcer. A miracle seed from a faraway mountain, it said, had halved the risk of heart attack, according to a new study. Lena, who had two months of beans and porridge behind her, felt the old pull of a shortcut, but she decided to ask Mr Bashir before she spent a penny.

That evening, Mr Bashir drew two circles on his chalkboard and joined them with an arrow, putting a food in the first circle and an illness in the second. A link between the two, he explained, can mean that the food causes the illness, that the illness changes what people eat, or that some third thing, such as age or income, influences both. Ice cream sales and sunburn rise together every summer, he added, but nobody thinks that ice cream burns people, because we can all see the sun standing behind both.

Many studies of food, Mr Bashir went on, are observational: they follow large groups of people for years, record what they eat and note who falls ill. Their great strength is size, since thousands of people can be followed for decades, and their great weakness is that people who eat well also tend to live differently in many other ways. Even so, he said, these studies are among the best tools that science has for questions that unfold slowly over many years.

People who eat plenty of vegetables, fruit and whole grains, he explained, also tend to smoke less, exercise more and see their doctor sooner, so researchers use statistics to adjust for such differences. The method works well for the things that were measured, but it cannot correct for what nobody thought to record, and a careful scientist always leaves some room for doubt. Lena wrote the word confounder in her notebook, and he told her that she would not need it often but would enjoy using it.

The best test of a cause is a randomised trial, in which chance decides who receives which treatment, so that the groups start out alike and only one thing differs between them. If the people given the extra beans are healthier at the end than the people who were not, the beans are a much more likely reason. Trials are not perfect, Mr Bashir added, but they remove many of the hidden differences that haunt the big surveys.

Trials of whole diets are hard to run, because people cannot easily hide what they eat, they find it hard to stick to a new menu for years, and the diseases in question often take decades to appear. For these reasons, scientists often combine short trials of one measurable thing, such as cholesterol or blood pressure, with long observational studies of real illness. Lena, who had imagined science as a straight road, began to see it as a patient process of fitting many small pieces together.

When laboratory work, trials, large surveys and basic biology all point in the same direction, Mr Bashir said, confidence grows, and this is why he trusts the advice to eat more vegetables, beans and whole grains. No single piece of evidence could settle the matter alone, but together they make a case that is hard to dismiss. A miracle seed, by contrast, usually rests on one study, one result and one very persuasive advertisement.

Headlines are fond of reporting that a risk has doubled, which sounds alarming until one asks how large the risk was to begin with. Mr Bashir asked Lena to imagine a risk of one in a thousand that doubles to two in a thousand: it is a real change, but it is still a small one. The difference between a relative change and an absolute one, he said, is the most useful piece of arithmetic that a reader can learn, because headlines almost never explain it.

By the end of the evening, Lena had written a list of questions and pinned it to her fridge beside the napkin. Was the study about people or mice, how many took part, who paid for it, was it published in a reputable journal, and have other researchers found the same thing? One study, Mr Bashir said, is a clue and never the last word, and the more surprising the claim, the more evidence it deserves.

Lena traced the headline back to its source and found a small experiment with a few dozen people, which had measured a single blood test and had said nothing about heart attacks at all. The newspaper had made a mountain out of a molehill, as Mr Bashir had predicted, and Tom, a little embarrassed, admitted that he had not read past the first paragraph. What struck Lena most was that Mr Bashir, whenever he did not know something, said so plainly, and that this made her trust him more rather than less.

In April, Mrs Costa's market stall was a painter's palette of red radishes, orange carrots, green spring cabbages and purple sprouting broccoli, and Lena stood in front of it for a long time. Mr Bashir, who had come along to carry the bags, explained that these colours come from natural pigments, and that many of them seem to have effects of their own in the body. The details are still being worked out, he said, but the practical lesson was already clear: a plate with many colours is a plate with many different substances.

Variety, Mr Bashir said, matters far more than any single so-called superfood, and the word itself has no scientific meaning: it is a marketing idea, used to sell goji berries, powders and a good deal else. No one food can carry the burden of a whole diet, he said, and a cheap cabbage often offers as much as an expensive tub of powder. Lena, who had been tempted by a green powder the week before, quietly put the thought away.

Blueberries, blackberries, red cabbage and purple carrots owe their rich colours to pigments called anthocyanins, which scientists are studying for possible effects on the heart and the brain. The results so far are interesting rather than conclusive, Mr Bashir warned, and one should enjoy berries for their taste and their fibre first. Frozen berries, he added, are cheap, keep most of their goodness and make a splendid cold topping for porridge in the morning.

Spinach, kale, chard and cabbage are rich in fibre, folate and vitamin K, and they cost very little when they are in season. Lena discovered that a handful of leaves, shredded into soup or wilted into pasta, almost disappears in the pan while it adds colour, texture and nutrients. Even the stalks of chard, which she had always thrown away, turned out to be delicious when they were chopped and fried with garlic.

Leafy greens come with one important caution, which Mr Bashir gave without being asked: vitamin K affects the blood-thinning medicine warfarin. Anyone who takes it should talk to their doctor before making a large change to the amount of leafy greens in their diet, and the usual advice is to keep the amount fairly steady. General advice, he said gently, can never replace the advice of someone who knows a patient's history.

Broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage and Brussels sprouts all belong to one plant family, and some large studies have linked eating them regularly with a lower risk of certain cancers. As always, Mr Bashir reminded her, such studies show a link and not proof, but the vegetables are good food in any case, and they cost little when they are in season. Lena found that roasted cauliflower, with a little oil and smoked paprika, tasted a good deal better than its reputation.

Boiling vegetables for a long time, Mr Bashir explained, can leave some of their water-soluble vitamins, such as vitamin C and folate, in the pan, whereas steaming, roasting and quick stir-frying keep more of them in the food. Where boiling is unavoidable, the cooking water makes a good base for soup, so that nothing is truly wasted. Lena poured the green water from her peas into a jug, and felt like a member of a very small and very sensible secret society.

Cooking is not always a loss, however, because heat helps the body to take up some compounds: the lycopene in tomatoes and the beta-carotene in carrots are absorbed better after cooking, and a little oil helps further. A salad dressed with a spoonful of olive oil, he said, may therefore bring more benefit than the same salad eaten dry. Lena, who had always eaten her salad dry out of a vague sense of virtue, was pleased to be told that she could stop.

Onions and garlic, Mr Bashir declared, are the foundation of half the world's cooking, and Lena learned to cook onions slowly in a little oil until they turned soft, golden and almost sweet. Once that base was ready, a tin of tomatoes, a handful of beans or a spoonful of spices could turn it into a meal in a quarter of an hour. She had once thought of cooking as a series of difficult tricks, but she now saw that it was mostly a matter of patience and a good onion.

On Saturday, Lena told Mrs Costa that her fridge tally had reached twenty different plants in a single week, and the stallholder laughed so loudly that two customers turned round to look. She pressed a free bunch of chard into Lena's hands and announced that in thirty years she had never had a better customer for it. Lena carried the leaves home like a trophy, and that evening she cooked a plate in every colour that the market had to offer.

Frozen vegetables, Mr Bashir told her, are usually picked at their best, blanched and frozen within hours, which locks in most of their nutrients and leaves them ready to cook with no washing or chopping. Lena opened her freezer drawer and saw it with new eyes: peas, spinach, mixed peppers and sweetcorn, all prepared and waiting for her. Nobody, she thought, could honestly call that a compromise, since it was cheaper, quicker and every bit as colourful as fresh.

Fresh, he went on, is not always best, because vegetables that spend days in lorries, warehouses and shop displays slowly lose some of their vitamin C and other delicate nutrients. A bag of peas frozen on the day of harvest may therefore compare well with a pod of peas that is a week old, though the difference is small and varies from food to food. A freezer drawer, he said with a grin, is a small insurance policy against takeaway menus.

Tinned tomatoes, beans, chickpeas and sweetcorn are similarly useful, because they are cooked in the can and keep for years, and the best ones are packed in water with no added salt or sugar. Mr Bashir showed Lena how to drain and rinse tinned beans in a sieve, which washes away part of the salt, and he added that tinned tomatoes are a rich source of lycopene. Her cupboard, she realised, was becoming a well-stocked shelter against the kind of tired evening that once ended in a takeaway.

Dried fruit, such as raisins, apricots and dates, counts as a portion in many guides, although a portion is only about 30 grams, because the water has been removed and the sugar is concentrated. It also sticks to the teeth, so it is best eaten with meals rather than nibbled all afternoon. Lena kept a small jar of raisins for her porridge and found that a few of them gave all the sweetness she needed.

An orange and a glass of orange juice are not the same food, Mr Bashir pointed out, because pressing the fruit removes most of its fibre and leaves the sugar free to be absorbed quickly. It also takes the work out of eating, so that a glass of juice holds the sugar of two or three oranges but fills the stomach far less than they would. Lena tried the experiment herself, ate one orange slowly at the kitchen table, and found that it was far more satisfying than the glass.

The World Health Organization advises that free sugars, a group that includes the sugar in fruit juice, honey and syrups as well as the sugar added to sweets, should make up less than ten percent of a person's daily energy. For an adult who eats about 2,000 calories a day, that is about 50 grams, or twelve teaspoons, and the same body says that going below five percent would bring further benefits. A single can of fizzy drink can easily contain more than half of the whole allowance.

Blending whole fruit into a smoothie breaks open the walls of its cells, and some national guides therefore count part of its sugar as free sugar, even though nothing has been added. A small glass of smoothie can be a pleasant treat, Mr Bashir said, but it is much easier to drink a great deal of fruit than to eat it. Lena, who preferred to chew, took her fruit whole and kept the blender for soup.

Walnuts, almonds, hazelnuts, cashews and similar nuts supply healthy unsaturated fats, protein, fibre and minerals, and many studies link a small daily handful, about 30 grams, with a lower risk of heart disease. Mr Bashir noted that the evidence comes mostly from large observational studies, together with trials showing that nuts improve cholesterol levels, so the picture is fairly consistent. Lena scattered chopped walnuts over her porridge and almonds over her salads, and found that a small amount added a great deal of flavour.

Nuts are rich in energy, so a handful is plenty, and plain ones are a better choice than salted, sugared or chocolate-coated nuts, which add a good deal of salt or sugar. Nut allergies can be serious, Mr Bashir reminded her, and whole nuts are a choking risk for children under five, so families should follow the advice of their doctor or nurse. Lena resolved never to bring nuts to a party without asking, a resolution that she thought would make her a better guest.

Seeds such as pumpkin, sunflower, flax and chia are small packets of fibre, minerals and healthy fats, and Lena began to add a spoonful to her porridge, her salads and her soups. Nut butters are useful too, Mr Bashir said, provided that the label lists nothing but nuts, because many brands add sugar, salt and cheap oils. By the end of April, her cupboard held so many jars and bags that it looked like a small shop, and she suspected that she was more pleased with it than was strictly sensible.

Fat is not the enemy, Mr Bashir said, as he drew three boxes on the chalkboard and labelled them unsaturated, saturated and trans. The body needs some fat for energy, for building cells and for absorbing certain vitamins, but the kind of fat matters a great deal more than the amount that appears on the front of a packet. Lena, who had spent years choosing products labelled low fat, felt a little foolish.

Olive oil, rapeseed oil, nuts, seeds and avocados are rich in unsaturated fats, while butter, cream, cheese and the fat of meat contain more saturated fat. Health bodies in many countries advise eating less of the saturated kind and more of the unsaturated, and the reasons have to do with the effect on cholesterol in the blood. Lena looked at the butter dish on her table, then at the bottle of olive oil beside it, and quietly moved one of them closer.

Coconut oil and palm oil, although they come from plants, are high in saturated fat, which is a good reminder that the word plant on a label does not settle the matter. Mr Bashir said that coconut in a curry is a delicious tradition and no cause for alarm, but that it makes no sense to treat a spoonful of coconut oil as a health food. Lena learned to look at the facts under the label and to ignore the picture of the palm tree.

Trials have shown that replacing some saturated fat with unsaturated fat lowers harmful cholesterol, and large studies link the same swap with a lower risk of heart disease. The detail matters, Mr Bashir stressed, because replacing saturated fat with refined carbohydrates, such as white bread or sugary snacks, does not give the same benefit. Swapping butter for jam on white toast, in other words, is not a victory for the heart.

Trans fats, which are made in factories by hardening liquid oils, are the one kind of fat that nearly every health body wants removed from food altogether. The World Health Organization has called for them to be eliminated, and many countries have banned or limited them, but older recipes and imported snacks may still contain them. Lena checked the labels in her cupboard for the words partially hydrogenated oil, and was relieved to find none.

Oil is healthy, but it is also one of the most energy-dense foods there is, and a careless pour can add hundreds of calories to a meal without anybody noticing. Lena began to measure it with a spoon rather than pouring it from the bottle, and she discovered that a good non-stick pan needs far less than she had been using. A little olive oil, Mr Bashir said, is a flavour as well as a fat, and should be treated with some respect.

In 2015, the cancer research agency of the World Health Organization reviewed hundreds of studies and concluded that eating processed meat, such as bacon, ham and sausages, is a cause of bowel cancer. It also judged red meat to be a probable cause, a weaker verdict that reflects the fact that the evidence is less certain. The announcement made headlines around the world, and Lena had to admit that she, too, had read them with a slightly sinking heart.

Mr Bashir took care to explain what such a ranking really means: it describes how strong the evidence is that something can cause cancer, and not how large the risk is. Processed meat sits in the same group as tobacco smoke, yet the danger from an occasional sausage is tiny compared with the danger from smoking, and the agency itself pointed this out. Without that distinction, he said, the headlines gave a picture that was frightening and badly out of proportion.

In the United Kingdom, official advice is that people who eat a lot of red and processed meat, about 90 grams or more a day, should cut down to about 70 grams, which is a modest portion. Mr Bashir did not ask Lena to give up meat entirely: he simply suggested that she eat less of it, keep the processed kind for rare occasions and let beans, vegetables, fish and eggs do more of the work. She noticed, with some surprise, that after a few weeks she hardly missed the sausages at all, and that her shopping bill had begun to shrink.

Fish and eggs, Mr Bashir reminded her, have a place in a plant-rich diet, because the aim is plants first and not plants only. Oily fish such as sardines, mackerel and salmon supply omega-3 fats, and health services in several countries advise eating one portion a week, so Lena added a tin of sardines to her Saturday lunch. She decided that her plate was beginning to look exactly like the paper on her fridge, which pleased her more than she liked to admit.

Protein is found in a great many plant foods, among them beans, lentils, tofu, nuts, seeds and even whole grains, and the old idea that they must be carefully combined at every meal has long been set aside. A varied diet over the course of a day, dietitians now agree, provides all the building blocks that the body needs. Lena, who had always imagined a plate without meat as a plate without protein, was both relieved and slightly embarrassed.

Most adults need a little less than one gram of protein for every kilogram of body weight each day, Mr Bashir explained, and many people in wealthy countries already eat more than that without trying. Older adults, athletes and people recovering from illness may need more, and they are better advised by a professional than by a neighbour over a garden fence, he added with a smile. For Lena, the lesson was that she could stop worrying about protein and concentrate on eating a wide mix of foods.

Lena bought her first block of tofu with some suspicion, pressed the water out of it between two plates and fried it in cubes. At first it tasted like a sponge, but when she marinated the next batch in soy sauce, garlic and ginger for an hour, it came out golden and savoury, with an agreeable chew. Mr Bashir, who had been eating tofu since long before it became fashionable, pronounced the result excellent and asked for a second helping.

Tempeh is a firm, nutty cake of fermented soya beans that comes originally from Indonesia, and miso is a salty paste made from fermented soya beans, used to flavour soups and sauces. Edamame, the young soya beans that are served in their pods, make a good snack with a pinch of salt. Lena began to understand that soya was not a single strange product but a whole family of traditional foods with centuries of kitchen history behind them.

Having heard alarming stories about soya on the internet, Lena asked Mr Bashir whether it was safe. He replied that moderate amounts of soya foods appear to be safe for most people, and that the old fear that they act like the human hormone oestrogen has not been borne out by research on ordinary diets. Anyone with a medical worry, such as a history of hormone-related cancer, or with a soya allergy, should ask their own doctor or specialist.

Ready-made meat substitutes, such as burgers, sausages and nuggets, vary enormously, Mr Bashir warned. Some are simple and nutritious, built on beans or soya or mushrooms, while others are salty, heavily processed and no healthier than the meat they replace, so the label is worth reading. Lena compared two packets of vegetable burgers in the supermarket and found that one had three times as much salt as the other.

Ultra-processed foods, such as many fizzy drinks, packaged snacks and ready meals, are industrial products made from ingredients and additives that rarely appear in a home kitchen. Mr Bashir asked Lena to go through her cupboards with a notebook, and she found more of them than she cared to admit, including a packet of sweet biscuits and several tubs of ready-made sauce. The exercise, he assured her, was meant to inform and not to shame, since almost everybody's cupboard holds a few such things.

Many large studies link diets high in ultra-processed foods with weight gain and poorer health, though such studies, as Mr Bashir reminded her, can only show a link. In a small trial in the United States in 2019, twenty adults who lived in a research ward ate about 500 calories a day more on an ultra-processed menu than on an unprocessed one. It is still debated whether the processing or the sugar, salt and fat is to blame, so his advice was not to panic but to let whole foods fill most of the plate.

Mr Bashir taught Lena to read a label like a detective: the ingredients are listed by weight, so the first few are the main ones, and a short list of words she recognises is usually a good sign. Some countries also print a colour code for fat, sugar and salt on the front of the pack, but the figures per 100 grams on the back are more useful for comparing one product with another. Lena spent twenty minutes in the supermarket aisle with her telephone as a calculator, and went home with a cheaper basket.

By the end of May, Lena had settled on a rule that she could remember: cook mostly from whole foods, enjoy convenient ones without guilt, and treat the label as a guide and not a verdict. Tinned beans and wholemeal bread are not crimes, Mr Bashir agreed, and a healthy diet is not a test of purity that one passes or fails. She stuck a new card to her fridge beside the napkin, and it read, in her own handwriting, mostly plants, mostly whole, mostly happy.

Too much salt raises blood pressure in many people, and high blood pressure is a main risk factor for heart disease and stroke. For that reason, the World Health Organization advises adults to eat less than 5 grams of salt a day, about one level teaspoon. Mr Bashir wrote the number on the chalkboard and added that most adults eat considerably more than that, and Lena, who had never once weighed her salt, decided to find out where hers was going.

Much of the salt that we eat, Mr Bashir explained, is already present in bread, sauces, soups, cheese, processed meat and takeaway meals, and in many rich countries it makes up the greater part of the total. The salt shaker is therefore a rather small villain, he said, and changing what goes into the shopping basket does far more good than hiding the shaker. Lena checked the labels on her bread and her tins, and was amazed by how much salt a single slice or a single can could hold.

The taste for salt, Mr Bashir promised her, is a habit, and habits can change. If a person reduces the amount slowly, the taste buds adjust within a few weeks, and the food that once seemed normal begins to taste too salty. Lena tried the experiment on her own soup, using a little less each week, and was startled to discover that after a month the old recipe made her thirsty.

Lemon juice, vinegar, garlic, chilli, fresh herbs and spices can make a dish taste vivid with hardly any salt at all, and toasting nuts and seeds in a dry pan deepens their flavour too. Tomato paste, mushrooms and slowly roasted onions add the savoury, meaty depth that cooks call umami, which makes a plant-based dish feel complete. Lena learned that a squeeze of lemon at the last moment does the work that a teaspoon of salt once did, and does it better.

Vegetables, fruit and beans are rich in potassium, a mineral that helps the body to balance the effect of salt on blood pressure, so a plant-rich diet helps on two fronts at once. Mr Bashir added an important exception: people with kidney disease are sometimes told to limit potassium, and for them a general rule can be wrong, so they should follow the advice of their own doctor or dietitian. Lena noted the point carefully, because it was becoming her favourite lesson of all: that a good rule for most people is not a rule for everyone.

Sugar hides in many foods that do not taste sweet, including pasta sauces, soups, bread, breakfast cereals and flavoured yoghurts, and a surprising number of savoury products contain more of it than anybody would put in a cup of tea. Lena was dismayed to find several teaspoons of it in her favourite tomato soup, and she began to read the figures per 100 grams with the grim attention of a detective. Cooking from simple ingredients, she realised, avoids most of the problem almost without effort.

On a label, sugar may appear under a dozen different names, among them glucose syrup, dextrose, maltose, honey and fruit juice concentrate, and when several of them are listed separately, the total can be larger than any one line suggests. If a product contains three or four sweeteners in the first half of the list, Mr Bashir said, it is probably much sweeter than it looks. Lena copied the names into her notebook, feeling that she had been given the key to a secret code.

Sweet things are not forbidden, Mr Bashir said, since treats are part of life and a diet that allows no pleasure rarely lasts. Lena kept her slice of cake on Sundays, ate fruit with yoghurt after her weekday meals and found that she enjoyed the cake more now that it was an occasion. The aim, he explained, is to make sweetness a pleasure rather than a habit.
