In 2023, the World Health Organization advised against using artificial sweeteners to control body weight, because the evidence suggests that they bring no lasting benefit and may carry some risks, although the research is still developing. Mr Bashir pointed out that the best way to enjoy less sugar is to get used to less sweetness, and that water, tea and fruit do the job without any controversy. Lena swapped her diet drink for sparkling water with a slice of lemon, and discovered that she did not miss the sweetness at all.

One Sunday afternoon, Lena made a tomato sauce from a tin of tomatoes, a chopped onion, two cloves of garlic and a handful of basil, and let it bubble gently for half an hour. When she compared it with the jar that she used to buy, she saw that the jar listed added sugar and a good deal more salt, and that her own version had cost less and tasted fresher. It was a small victory, but it was the kind that Mr Bashir loved best, because it needed no willpower at all.

In early June, Lena decided that the neglected corner of her garden, where nothing had grown for years except nettles and a broken flowerpot, would become a vegetable bed. Mr Bashir lent her a spade, a barrow of compost and a great deal of advice, the most important piece of which was that most vegetables need about six hours of sun a day. She dug for a whole Saturday and went to bed with aching arms and a deep, unfamiliar satisfaction.

For her first year, Lena chose forgiving plants: radishes, salad leaves, runner beans, courgettes and a few pots of herbs. Mr Bashir, who believed that nobody should begin with an empty bed, also gave her a row of his own young pea plants, which he had raised in trays on his windowsill. She planted them with great care and a little ceremony, as if she were burying treasure.

Beans, Mr Bashir told her, have a secret that delights him every year: bacteria living in small nodules on their roots capture nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form that the plant can use. As a result, beans and their relatives help to feed the soil as well as the cook, and farmers have used them in crop rotations for centuries. Lena looked at her small row of beans with new respect, as though they were quietly running a fertiliser factory under the soil.

Then began the long business of waiting, and Lena watered her seedlings every evening and inspected them every morning, and found it harder than any recipe. One morning she discovered that slugs had eaten every lettuce in the bed, leaving only a few shiny trails behind. Mr Bashir, who listened to her lament with great sympathy and very little surprise, assured her that every gardener has lost a lettuce and that the survivors always taste better.

Herbs, he said, are the easiest plants for a beginner, because they grow well in pots on a sunny windowsill or beside the kitchen door, and a handful of fresh leaves can change a whole meal. Mint spreads so aggressively that it can take over a bed, so Lena kept it in a pot of its own, alongside parsley, basil, chives and coriander. Within a fortnight she was snipping herbs into everything, from scrambled eggs to bean salad, with the delight of a person who has found a free ingredient.

Gardening turned out to be good exercise as well as good food: digging, raking, carrying water and bending down all count as gentle physical activity, and doing them outdoors made them feel less like a chore. Lena enjoyed the fresh air and the daylight, and on warm evenings she found that she slept better after hours spent outside. None of this had anything to do with vegetables, as Mr Bashir cheerfully pointed out, and yet it was one of the best reasons to have a garden.

Mr Bashir also grew rhubarb in a sunny corner, and he warned Lena that although the pink stalks are safe to cook and eat, the large green leaves are poisonous, because they contain oxalic acid and other harmful substances. He cut them off at once, as he did every time, and put them on the compost heap, which was the only place for them. Safety in the kitchen garden, he said, is mostly a matter of knowing which part of the plant to eat.

On a warm afternoon, Lena picked a pea pod, split it with her thumbnail and ate the peas straight from the plant, and she stood there in surprise, because she had never tasted anything so sweet. Peas begin to turn their sugar into starch soon after picking, Mr Bashir explained, which is why the ones from a garden taste so different from those in a shop. Most of her first harvest, to be honest, never reached the kitchen at all, and she did not feel the least bit guilty.

After four weeks, the radishes were ready, and Lena made her first salad from her own radishes, salad leaves and herbs, dressed with lemon juice and a little olive oil. It was a small salad, and a few of the leaves had been nibbled by something other than herself, but she photographed it as proudly as if it were a banquet. Food that she had grown herself, she found, tasted remarkable, and she was far more willing to eat what she had watched grow.

On the longest evening of the year, Lena and Mr Bashir ate dinner at a small table among the vegetable beds, with the sun going down slowly behind the fence. He brought a bottle of olive oil and a loaf of wholemeal bread, she brought a bowl of beans cooked with garlic and herbs, and the radishes tasted of pepper and sunshine. Neither of them said very much, which, Lena decided, was the best compliment that a meal could receive.

At the end of June, Lena added up her receipts for the month and discovered, with real pleasure, that her new way of eating cost less than the old one. Prices differ between shops and countries, Mr Bashir cautioned, and a diet built on expensive substitutes can cost more rather than less, but plant foods in their simple forms are often cheaper than meat and fish. He nodded with satisfaction, because he had long held that a healthy diet should never be a luxury.

The cheapest foods in most shops, Mr Bashir said, are the very ones that dietitians like best: dried beans, lentils, oats, rice, cabbage, carrots, onions and bananas. Frozen vegetables and tinned tomatoes are also good value, and since all of these keep for a long time, they make a pantry that protects both the wallet and the diet. Lena wrote the list on the back of her shopping list, and felt a little like a general planning a very modest campaign.

When Lena looked at her old receipts, she saw where the money had gone: meat, fish, branded convenience foods, takeaway meals and snacks bought in a hurry, all of which cost far more per portion than a pot of lentils. Mr Bashir warned her that ready-made meat substitutes can be expensive too, so the cheapest plan is built on simple foods and not on clever packets. The tidy sums at the bottom of the page made a stronger argument than any lecture.

Planning, Mr Bashir said, is the quiet secret of a good diet, and every Sunday Lena sketched a week of meals before she wrote her shopping list. She bought fewer impulse snacks, wasted less food and always kept a supply of tinned beans, frozen vegetables, oats and rice in reserve for evenings when she was too tired to think. The list was plain and unglamorous, but it turned good intentions into groceries, and groceries into dinner.

Lena stopped throwing away broccoli stalks, soft carrots and the leaves of celery, and put them in a pot with an onion and some water to make the base for a soup. Mr Bashir, who disliked waste with great passion, explained that using food well saves money and also saves the water, land and energy that went into producing it. A bin that was half as full as before, she found, was a surprisingly satisfying sight.

A use-by date, Mr Bashir explained, is about safety, and food should not be eaten after it, whereas a best-before date is only about quality, and food past that date is often still fine if it looks and smells normal. Lena began to freeze her bread before it went stale and to slice overripe bananas into a freezer bag for porridge and smoothies, and she labelled every box with the date. The freezer, once a graveyard of forgotten things, became the most useful room in the house.

On Sunday afternoons, Lena discovered the pleasure of batch cooking: she made a large pot of soup, stew or curry once, divided it into boxes and froze most of it for the weeks ahead. The cooking took no longer than a normal meal, and the washing-up was done only once, which Mr Bashir described as the most underrated advantage of the method. By the third Sunday, she had a freezer full of coloured boxes, each with a handwritten label, and she felt oddly rich.

Batch cooking, Mr Bashir said, comes with rules that are worth learning: cool the food quickly, keep it in the fridge for two days at most, and reheat it until it is steaming hot. Rice needs special care, because the bacteria that it can carry produce toxins that survive reheating, so it should be cooled within an hour, kept in the fridge for no longer than a day and reheated only once. Lena wrote the rules on a card and stuck it inside the cupboard door.

Good cooking needs very little equipment, Mr Bashir insisted: a sharp knife, a large pot, a baking tray and a blender will do for most meals, and a sharp knife is safer than a blunt one. He then lent her his old pressure cooker, which cooks dried beans in a fraction of the usual time, and spent a quarter of an hour showing her how to use it safely. Lena took it home and set it on the stove with the solemnity of someone who has been handed a family heirloom.

On a tired Wednesday evening, Lena came home late, took a box of lentil soup out of the freezer and heated it while she sliced a loaf of wholemeal bread. Ten minutes later she was eating a hot and wholesome supper, and she thought, with a small smile, that Sunday Lena had given Wednesday Lena a very good present. It was a thought that she would have found absurd in January, and she enjoyed it all the more because of that.

Every week, Lena bought a new spice for her shelf, beginning with cumin and coriander seed and moving on to turmeric, smoked paprika, cardamom and a small tin of chilli flakes that she treated with great respect. Plain beans and boiled vegetables, she learned, are dull only until they meet a well-stocked spice shelf, and her cooking improved the moment she began to use it. Each week the kitchen smelled a little more interesting, and she began to look forward to the cooking more than the eating.

Mr Bashir showed her a trick that is used in kitchens across India: warm whole spices in a little hot oil for a few seconds, until they begin to sizzle and smell, and only then add the onions. The oil carries the flavour through the whole dish, and the result tastes far deeper than the same spices stirred in at the end. Lena practised until she could do it without burning anything, which took three attempts and one smoke alarm.

Many great cuisines grew up around exactly this skill, Mr Bashir pointed out: the dals of India, the lentil stews of Ethiopia, the beans of Mexico, the hummus of the Middle East and the tofu of Japan. Each of them turns modest and inexpensive plant foods into something delicious through flavour rather than expense. Lena began to think of her small kitchen as a place with a world map on its wall.

One Thursday, Lena's friend Dara, who had eaten no animal foods for several years, came round for dinner and offered to teach her how to make a proper lentil dal. Dara was a cheerful, practical woman who taught at the school down the road and who carried a small jar of her own spice mix in her bag, in case of emergencies. Lena, who had been cooking from recipes for months without ever meeting anyone who simply knew how to do it, accepted at once.

Dara fried cumin seeds, a chopped onion, garlic and fresh ginger until the kitchen smelled wonderful, and then added red lentils, tomatoes, turmeric and water, and left everything to simmer. Half an hour later, they ate a golden dal with brown rice and a squeeze of lemon, and Lena asked for the recipe, which Dara said did not exist, because she had never once measured anything. The two women wrote one down together anyway, with the amounts guessed as carefully as possible.

Over dinner, Dara explained that she had chosen a fully plant-based diet mainly out of concern for animals, and Lena listened with interest and without argument. Lena had not made the same choice, and she said so honestly, but they agreed that a good meal can be shared without agreeing about everything. Mr Bashir, when he heard about the evening, remarked that the table is one of the oldest places in the world for being polite to people who think differently.

Dara sprinkled turmeric into almost everything she cooked, and Lena wondered aloud whether it was a cure for disease, since she had read somewhere that it was. Mr Bashir explained that its pigment, curcumin, has been studied in some human trials, but the results are mixed and the body absorbs it poorly, so a pinch on the dinner has little proven effect. It is a lovely spice, he said, and it is quite enough to enjoy it as one.

Ginger, garlic and chilli give simple beans and vegetables a great deal of flavour, and they are cheap, easy to find and easy to grow in a pot on a windowsill. Research on their possible health effects is interesting, Mr Bashir said, and some of it may prove useful one day, but the best reason to use them is that they make a meal taste wonderful. Lena found that she was now buying a knob of fresh ginger every week, as automatically as she once bought a packet of biscuits.

In the heat of July, Lena turned to cold dishes that needed almost no cooking: a bean salad with tomatoes, cucumber, herbs and lemon, a chilled tomato soup and a bowl of couscous with chickpeas and roasted peppers. She ate them outdoors in the evening sun, and she hardly needed to turn on the oven all week. Salad, she discovered, is not a punishment when it is made with beans, nuts, herbs and a good dressing.

Some vegetables, such as rocket, radicchio and chicory, taste bitter, and many people, especially children, dislike them at first, but a squeeze of lemon or a spoonful of olive oil makes the bitterness gentler. Lena was practising this lesson on a salad one Friday when her telephone rang, and her brother Jonas, sounding cheerful, invited her to his birthday barbecue on Saturday. She agreed at once, and then stood in the kitchen wondering what on earth she would eat.

On Saturday afternoon, Lena arrived at Jonas's garden with a large bean salad, a tray of vegetable skewers threaded with peppers, mushrooms, courgettes and onions, and a bag of corn on the cob. The lawn was full of friends, balloons and drifting smoke, and her small niece Maya ran up to inspect what she had brought with the frank suspicion of a customs officer. Lena handed over the bags with a nervous smile and wondered how the afternoon would go.

A friend of Jonas's, balancing a paper plate on one knee, asked Lena whether she had become a vegan, and she explained cheerfully that she was simply eating more plants. The man shrugged, took a skewer from the tray and announced that it looked a good deal better than the sausages. It was the end of the matter, and Lena realised that she had been dreading a conversation that nobody else had any interest in having.

Lena filled her plate with vegetable skewers, bean salad and corn, took a small piece of grilled chicken to be polite, and discovered that nobody was watching her plate at all. Mr Bashir had warned her that all-or-nothing rules are a poor plan, because the best diet is the one that a person can enjoy and keep for years. Food, he liked to say, is also about friends, memory and pleasure, and a healthy way of eating has room for all three.

Jonas took great care at the barbecue, cooking the chicken right through, using separate plates and tongs for raw and cooked meat, and keeping the salads in the shade. Lena remembered Mr Bashir's rule that food should not stay out for more than two hours, or one hour on a very hot day, and she quietly carried the bean salad back to the fridge in relays. Safe cooking, she reflected, is not a matter of worry but of habit, like putting on a seat belt.

Meat that is heavily charred, Mr Bashir had told her, contains chemicals that worry scientists, and so Jonas scraped off the black parts and kept the flames low. Vegetables on a grill do not form the same chemicals, although they too taste best when they are browned and not blackened, and a little oil and a few herbs make them irresistible. It was a small example of how the pleasures of cooking and the advice of experts can sometimes point in the same direction.

When Jonas offered her a beer, Lena asked for sparkling water with lemon and ice, and she explained quietly that she was trying to drink less. Mr Bashir had told her that the World Health Organization says no amount of alcohol is completely safe for health, and that the old story about red wine and the heart is much weaker than it sounds. Official advice in the United Kingdom is to drink no more than fourteen units a week, spread over several days, but that is a ceiling rather than a target.

Maya, who was five and had firm opinions, walked past the salad, the skewers and the watermelon and asked for plain bread, and nothing that anybody said could change her mind. Jonas rolled his eyes and told Lena that his daughter had refused every green thing for a month, and that he had run out of both patience and ideas. Lena watched the small determined face and made a mental note, because she suspected that Mr Bashir would have something to say about it.

The skewers, the corn and a great bowl of watermelon were the first things to disappear from the table, and several guests came to ask Lena for the recipe for the bean salad. Jonas, who had declared that morning that he would eat nothing without a sausage in it, took seconds of everything and licked his fingers like a boy. Lena felt the quiet glow of a cook whose food has been eaten rather than merely tolerated.

Later, in the kitchen, Jonas lowered his voice and told Lena that his doctor had said his cholesterol was high, and he asked her what he ought to eat. Lena, remembering what Mr Bashir had taught her about the limits of advice, said that she was not an expert and that he should ask his doctor or a registered dietitian, but she offered to share her recipes. It was the first time that she had understood that knowing when to say I do not know is part of knowing something.

As the sun went down, Maya fell asleep on a blanket under the apple tree, and Lena helped Jonas with the washing-up while the last of the guests said goodbye. She ate a large slice of birthday cake with great pleasure, because Mr Bashir had taught her that treats are part of life and that the best diet is the one that a person can enjoy and keep. It had been, she decided, a very good day, and she had not once felt that she was on a diet.

Vitamin B12 is the one nutrient that every fully plant-based eater must plan for, Mr Bashir explained, because it is made by bacteria and is found naturally in meat, fish, eggs and dairy foods but not reliably in plants. Fortified foods, such as some plant milks, breakfast cereals and yeast extracts, can supply it, and so can a supplement. The right choice and the right dose, he added, are matters for a doctor or a registered dietitian and not for a neighbour with a spade.

The body needs vitamin B12 to make healthy red blood cells and to protect the nerves, and a shortage can cause a form of anaemia and, if it goes on, lasting damage to the nerves. Because the liver stores a generous supply, it may take years for a deficiency to show, which is why people who change their diet sometimes feel perfectly well until the reserves are gone. Mr Bashir stressed that this is easy to prevent and that prevention is far better than cure.

Dara took a vitamin B12 supplement every day and had her blood checked once a year, and she told Lena that it had become as ordinary a part of her routine as brushing her teeth. Lena still ate eggs and dairy foods, so she was at lower risk, but Mr Bashir wanted her to know that older adults and people on certain medicines may need extra B12. For all of them, he repeated, a blood test and a professional are the way to find out.

Beans, lentils, tofu, nuts, seeds and leafy greens all contain iron, but the body absorbs the iron in plants less easily than the iron in meat, so people who eat little animal food should pay attention to it. Vitamin C from fruit and vegetables helps the body to take it up, so a squeeze of lemon on a lentil dish does a useful job, while tea and coffee drunk with a meal can reduce the absorption. Lena began to see her plate as a small team in which every food had a part to play.

Calcium, which builds and protects bones and teeth, is found in kale, bok choy, almonds, sesame seeds, tofu that has been set with calcium and plant milks that have had it added. Spinach contains a great deal of calcium on paper, but it also contains oxalate, which binds the mineral and stops the body from absorbing most of it, and not every plant milk is fortified. Lena checked the carton in her fridge, and was pleased to find that the label told her exactly what she wanted to know.

Iodine is needed to make the hormones of the thyroid gland, and in many countries the main sources are milk, dairy foods and fish, so people who avoid them should take care to find it elsewhere. Plant milks are often not fortified with iodine, and the iodine content of seaweed varies so enormously that some kinds contain far more than is wise, which makes it unreliable as a regular source. Iodised salt can help, Mr Bashir said, but since the aim is to eat less salt, a conversation with a dietitian is the best next step.

In summer, sunlight on the skin helps the body to make vitamin D, which is needed for strong bones, but in the darker months of the year in countries far from the equator this works poorly, whatever one eats. Many health bodies therefore advise a vitamin D supplement for most people during autumn and winter, and few foods contain much of it naturally, apart from oily fish, eggs and some mushrooms that have been exposed to light. Mr Bashir, who was past seventy, said that he took one himself, on the advice of his own doctor.

Walnuts, ground flax seeds, chia seeds and rapeseed oil contain an omega-3 fat called ALA, which the body needs but cannot make for itself. It converts only a little of this into the longer omega-3 fats, known as EPA and DHA, that are found in oily fish, so people who eat no fish sometimes choose a supplement made from algae. Whether such a supplement is needed, Mr Bashir said, depends on the person, and the question is worth taking to a professional.

To see how it all fits together, Lena sketched a day's menu on the back of an envelope: porridge with seeds and fortified plant milk, lentil soup with an orange, and tofu with greens and brown rice. Beans, seeds and whole grains also supply zinc, Mr Bashir added, although it is easier to absorb when they have been soaked or sprouted, and a varied plate makes up for most small gaps. She looked at her menu with the satisfaction of a person who has solved a puzzle that turned out to be less difficult than it looked.

What worried Lena most was the thought of getting something wrong, and Mr Bashir told her that the safest way to deal with any worry about nutrients is to look and not to guess. A blood test can show whether someone is low in iron, vitamin B12 or vitamin D, he said, and nobody should take high doses of supplements without advice, because some vitamins build up in the body. Lena put her worries away with the envelope, and made a note to ask her own doctor at her next check-up.

Babies and young children, Mr Bashir explained, need plenty of energy and nutrients for their rapid growth, and their stomachs are small, so the way they are fed deserves careful planning. Some national dietetic bodies say that well-planned plant-based diets can suit every stage of life, including childhood, but the key word is well-planned, and a parent who wishes to try one should ask a doctor or a registered dietitian first. Health services in some countries also advise vitamin supplements for young children, whatever their diet.

During pregnancy a woman needs more of several nutrients, and doctors in many countries advise folic acid before conception and in the early weeks, because it helps to protect the baby against certain defects of the spine and brain. Any large change of diet at that time, Mr Bashir said, should be discussed with a doctor, a midwife or a dietitian, since both too little and too much of some nutrients can cause harm. Lena, who was not pregnant, wrote the point down anyway, because she had friends who might be one day.

Mr Bashir, who was past seventy, explained that older adults often have smaller appetites and absorb some nutrients less well, and so they need to make every mouthful count. He took vitamin D and B12 on his doctor's advice and made a point of eating protein at every meal, from beans, fish, eggs and a little yoghurt. Growing old, he said with a smile, is not a reason to stop eating well, but it is a good reason to ask for a little help.

Some illnesses change what a person should eat, and for them a general rule can be wrong: people with kidney disease may need to limit potassium and phosphorus, which are plentiful in some beans, nuts and leafy greens. Some people with diabetes must match their food to their medicines, and some people with irritable bowel syndrome find that beans and onions upset them. Medicines can also interact with foods, as grapefruit does with several common tablets, so Mr Bashir tells anyone on regular medicine to ask their pharmacist or doctor whether any foods matter.

Mr Bashir spoke more quietly when he came to the next subject, which was the way in which a healthy interest in food can sometimes become an unhealthy one. Anyone whose thoughts about food have become anxious or controlling, or who has had an eating disorder in the past, should speak to a doctor rather than rely on advice from a friend or the internet. Eating more plants, he said, should be a pleasure and a freedom, and it should never become a rulebook that causes fear.

In some countries, dietitian is a protected title, which means that a registered dietitian has studied for years, works to professional standards and can be held to account. The word nutritionist is not protected everywhere, so Mr Bashir suggested that Lena should always ask about a person's training before she took their advice. A good professional, he added, will explain the evidence, admit what is uncertain and never promise a miracle.

Once a month, Mr Bashir volunteered at a community health centre, and one Saturday morning Lena went with him to carry boxes of fruit and to watch. A tired mother with a small child sat down at his table, and he did not give orders or recite rules, but listened for a long while and asked a few quiet questions. Lena realised that the best advice is often a good question, and that he was better at it than anyone she had ever met.

Nuts, peanuts, soya, sesame, celery, mustard and several other foods are common causes of allergy, and some allergic reactions can be serious or even dangerous. People with allergies must read every label, ask about ingredients when they eat out, and follow the plan that their doctor has given them. Lena, who had cheerfully added tahini and almonds to half her recipes, resolved to ask her guests before she cooked for them.

Plant foods are bulky and filling for their energy, so growing teenagers, very active people and some older adults may need extra energy from nuts, seeds, oils, avocados and whole grains. Mr Bashir pointed out that a diet that is perfect for a desk worker may leave a young footballer hungry and tired, and that the body usually says so clearly. Anyone who loses weight without trying, he added, should see a doctor, since that can be a sign of illness and never a reason for congratulation.

On the way home, Lena wrote a list of questions to ask her own doctor at her next check-up, and she felt oddly proud of it, since in January she would not have known what to ask. Mr Bashir, at the wheel, remarked that knowing when to ask an expert is one of the skills of eating well, and that nobody is born with it. She added a last line to the list, in capital letters, that said what else should I know, and she underlined it twice.

Water remains the simplest and best everyday drink, Mr Bashir said, and how much a person needs depends on their size, the weather and how active they are, so thirst and pale urine are better guides than any fixed number. Fruit, vegetables and soups also contribute a good deal of water, which surprised Lena. She put a jug of water with lemon and mint in the middle of the table, and noticed that she drank more of it without even trying.

Unsweetened tea and coffee, taken in moderation, are fine for most people, Mr Bashir said, and tea in particular contains plant substances called flavonoids that scientists are studying. Too much caffeine can disturb sleep and should be limited in pregnancy, so Lena stopped drinking coffee after lunch and found that she slept more deeply. Whatever was in the cup, he reminded her, a heap of sugar and a mountain of cream turn a healthy drink into a pudding.

Sugary soft drinks supply a great deal of sugar and almost nothing else, Mr Bashir said, and fruit juice is best kept to one small glass a day, since it is also a concentrated source of free sugars. Milk and unsweetened plant milks make good drinks, provided that the plant milk is fortified with calcium and, ideally, with vitamin B12 and iodine. Lena discovered that she could easily replace her afternoon cola with a mug of herbal tea and a handful of nuts.

Yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and miso are fermented foods, and many of them contain live bacteria that may support the gut and the body's defences. Mr Bashir warned, however, that heat treatment after fermentation kills the bacteria, so shelf-stable jars of sauerkraut and some pasteurised products no longer contain them, and that some fermented foods are very salty. Lena stirred a spoonful of fresh sauerkraut into her lunch, simply because she liked its sharp taste.

In a small trial in the United States, a few dozen adults who ate plenty of fermented foods for ten weeks showed more varied gut microbes and lower levels of some markers of inflammation than they had at the start. It was a short trial with few people, Mr Bashir noted, so it is a promising signal rather than a verdict, and he called fermented foods a tasty extra rather than a cure. Probiotic pills are a different matter, with mixed evidence, and only a few particular strains have been shown to help with specific conditions.

Several studies have found that people who eat plenty of vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains are less likely to report feeling depressed. Some scientists suspect that the gut and the brain influence one another, but almost all of these studies are observational, however, so they show a link that may partly reflect other differences in people's lives. Mr Bashir described the research as active but young, and he took care not to say anything that sounded like a promise.

A small trial in Australia found that adults with depression who were helped to follow a Mediterranean-style diet improved more than a comparison group, which is encouraging, although more research is needed. Mr Bashir described this as a hope rather than a promise, and he insisted that anyone who feels low for weeks on end should speak to a doctor rather than rely on a menu. Food may be a friend to the mind, he said, but it is not a substitute for care.

Standing in front of a shelf of vitamin pills and powders at the chemist, Lena asked Mr Bashir whether she ought to be buying any of them. For most healthy people, he answered, a varied diet is the better investment, because foods contain fibre and countless other compounds that a tablet cannot copy, and trials of general multivitamins have not shown clear protection against disease. Lena left the shop with a packet of mints and a feeling of unexpected thrift.

The history of supplements, he said, holds a warning: in the 1990s two large trials found that smokers who took beta-carotene pills had more lung cancer, not less, though foods rich in it seemed healthy. A nutrient eaten inside a carrot and the same nutrient swallowed alone in a high dose, in other words, are not necessarily the same thing. Some people do need a particular supplement, such as vitamin B12 or vitamin D, but that is a decision for a doctor or dietitian, based on the person and not on the shelf.

A glossy magazine advertised a detox tea that promised to wash the poisons out of the body in seven days, and Mr Bashir, reading it over the fence, laughed until he had to wipe his glasses. The liver, kidneys, lungs and skin, he explained, are already excellent at clearing waste, and there is no good evidence that any tea or juice cleanse does the job better. Some products sold for detox contain laxatives or herbs that can interact with medicines, so the best detox plan, in his dry opinion, is the plain one of eating more plants and drinking enough water.

In October, Lena kept her food diary for a second week and laid it beside the one she had written in January, and the difference was plain to see. The first notebook had been a story of bread, pasta, cheese and ready meals, written by someone who was too busy to look at what she was eating. The second was the story of a cook, and she read it with a small shock of recognition.

Vegetables, beans, oats and fruit now filled the pages, with nuts and seeds scattered like punctuation, and the ready meals had almost vanished. Her fridge tally, which she had never stopped keeping, now regularly reached thirty different plants in a week, which was the number from the survey that Mr Bashir had once mentioned. She counted them twice, to be sure, and then laughed at herself for needing to.

Lena did not claim to feel transformed, and a slice of cake and a plate of cheese still appeared on Sundays, as they always would. What had changed was quieter and, she suspected, more lasting: she cooked more, spent less and no longer thought of eating well as a punishment. Mr Bashir, when she showed him the two notebooks, studied them for a long time and said that it was the most convincing piece of evidence he had seen all year, though only for a study of one.

On a Saturday in October, Jonas brought Maya to lunch, and Lena served a tray of roasted broccoli beside a pot of pasta with lentil sauce. Maya, who was fully aware of her reputation, pushed the broccoli to the very edge of her plate and announced that green things are for rabbits. Jonas gave Lena a look that said he had warned her, and Lena, with a calm that surprised even herself, said nothing at all.

When Lena asked Mr Bashir for advice, he told her that children often need to meet a new food again and again, sometimes ten times or more, before they accept it. A child who refuses a food today has not failed, he said, and neither has the parent, because taste is partly learned and familiarity is the great teacher. The trick, in his experience, is to keep offering the food in a relaxed way without ever making a battle of it.

Calm repetition works far better than pressure, he explained, and small portions, good examples and eating together at the table all help, whereas bribes, bargains and begging usually backfire. In particular, dessert should not be offered as a prize for finishing the vegetables, since that teaches a child that vegetables are a chore and sweets are a reward. Lena put one small piece of broccoli on Maya's plate at the next meal, and she said not a word about it.

The following weekend, Maya helped Lena to cut a head of broccoli into little trees, toss them in oil with a pinch of garlic and lay them on a baking tray, while Lena looked after the hot oven. When they came out crisp and golden at the edges, Maya inspected one with great suspicion, sniffed it, and bit off the top as though it were a very small tree indeed. There was a long silence, and then she announced that it tasted like a crisp, which Lena accepted as the highest praise that had ever been paid to a vegetable.

A good diet, Mr Bashir reminded her on the doorstep, is no replacement for regular health checks, because high blood pressure, raised cholesterol and high blood sugar often cause no symptoms at first and can be found only by measuring. A person can feel entirely well, eat beautifully and still have a number that deserves attention. Lena listened carefully, because the idea that one can look and feel healthy while something quiet is going on was a good deal more serious than anything he had told her about broccoli.

Lena booked an appointment with her doctor, Dr Patel, partly out of curiosity and partly because she had promised Mr Bashir that she would. The doctor measured her blood pressure, took a small sample of blood and asked her a few friendly questions about her diet, her sleep and her exercise, and Lena took out her list and asked a few of her own. The visit was quick and unremarkable, which, as the nurse said with a smile as she handed over the form, is exactly what everybody hopes for.

On Sunday evening, Jonas telephoned with two pieces of news that made Lena smile for the rest of the night. Maya had asked for more little trees at dinner, without being asked and without being bribed, and he had made an appointment with a registered dietitian to talk about his cholesterol. It was, he said, a small step, but Lena had learned from Mr Bashir that small steps are the ones that last.

Over many years, studies of Mediterranean-style diets and of other eating patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains and nuts have repeatedly linked them with a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers. None of this is a guarantee for any single person, Mr Bashir cautioned, and a link, as he had said so often, is not proof. What impressed him was the consistency of the picture, which had held for decades across different countries and different kinds of research.

One of the best-known trials, he said, was PREDIMED in Spain, where adults at high risk of heart disease were given extra olive oil or nuts and had fewer heart attacks and strokes than a comparison group. The paper was corrected and published again in 2018 after problems were found in how some participants had been assigned, and the new analysis gave broadly similar results. Mr Bashir liked the story, because it showed science doing what science should do: checking its own work and admitting its mistakes.

Even so, the details of the best diet are still argued over by scientists, who rarely agree about the small print: how much fat, how many carbohydrates, how much dairy, how much fish. Mr Bashir regarded this as healthy rather than alarming, because disagreement about the margins is normal in a living science, while agreement about the main shape is what matters. Eat mostly plants, he said, in as much variety as you can manage, and do not let the arguments about the rest spoil your dinner.

Food is only one part of a healthy life, Mr Bashir reminded her, and a perfect diet cannot make up for poor sleep, a lack of movement, smoking or a life with no friends in it. Genes, luck and circumstances play a part too, which means that nobody controls every piece of their own health, and nobody should feel guilty about the pieces that they do not. Lena took this as a relief, and she went for a long walk with Dara that evening, talking about nothing in particular.

Big plans collapse, Mr Bashir said, while small habits tend to survive, so he advised anyone who wants to eat more plants to add one new plant-based meal a week and keep only the ones they enjoy. After a year, the gentle method adds up to dozens of new recipes, without a single dramatic resolution or a single day of misery. It was, he admitted, the least glamorous advice that he had ever given, and also the only kind that he had ever seen work.

Lena stuck a calendar to the fridge and put a small green tick on every Monday on which she had cooked something new, and by December the ticks marched across the page like a row of small green soldiers. Behind them stood a notebook of recipes, a freezer full of labelled boxes, a garden bed that was empty now and waiting for spring, and a fridge tally that no longer surprised her. She realised that she had made one decision in January and almost none since, and yet she had changed nearly everything.

In December, Lena invited her friends and Mr Bashir to dinner, and she spent the afternoon in a kitchen that smelled of cumin, garlic and baking apples. She made a rich lentil stew, a tray of roasted winter vegetables glistening with oil and herbs, and baked apples stuffed with chopped nuts and cinnamon, and she lit candles on the table because the evening seemed to deserve them. For a moment, standing at the stove with a wooden spoon, she remembered the grey fridge of January and nearly laughed aloud.

Dara, Jonas, Maya, Tom and Mr Bashir crowded around the table, and the kitchen grew warm with talk, laughter and steam from the stew. Nobody remarked that the meal was plant-based until the plates were almost empty, at which point Tom, who had once sent Lena a headline about a miracle seed, asked in a puzzled voice where the meat had been. Lena only smiled, passed him the bread and said that he had not missed it.

Jonas asked for seconds and for the recipes, and he told the table that he had started a plan with a registered dietitian and that his next blood test would show how well it was working. Maya, who had been given a small bowl of roasted broccoli, ate three little trees without being asked and announced that they were nearly as good as chips. Mr Bashir lifted his glass of water and offered the toast that everyone at the table now knew by heart: a link is not proof.

As the year ended, Lena and Mr Bashir sat over a pot of tea and agreed that eating more plants is a direction rather than a test, and that the best change is the one that lasts. This book gives general information only and is not medical advice, so anyone with a health condition, an allergy, a pregnancy or a special diet should ask a doctor or a registered dietitian before making changes. For everyone else, the next step is small and delicious: put one more plant on tomorrow's plate.
